name: Authlib JOSE (Python)
description: The JOSE component of the Authlib suite

ecosystem.comment: Pure CPython package, requires_python >=3.10. No bindings for other runtimes.

license.comment: PyPI metadata and the GitHub license field both report BSD-3-Clause. The project additionally sells a commercial licence for closed-source use, but the open-source terms are BSD-3-Clause.

implementation.comment: HMAC uses CPython's stdlib `hmac`/`hashlib` (including `hmac.compare_digest`); all asymmetric and AEAD work is delegated to pyca/cryptography, which is an FFI/Rust binding over OpenSSL. Examined Authlib 1.7.2.

repository.comment: The JOSE code lives under `authlib/jose/` in the main Authlib repository; it is not shipped as a separate distribution.

package.comment: No standalone package — `authlib.jose` ships inside the Authlib distribution.

documentation.comment: The JOSE section of the Authlib docs carries a prominent deprecation banner pointing at joserfc.

first-release.comment: First PyPI upload 0.1rc0 on 2017-10-25; repository created 2017-10-27. The JOSE module has been part of the distribution since the early releases.

latest-version.comment: 1.7.2, released 2026-05-06 (checked 2026-07-30). `authlib.jose` is deprecated as of 1.7.0 and is announced for removal in 1.8.

hmac-hs.comment: `HMACAlgorithm(256|384|512)` in JWS_ALGORITHMS, all three in the default `jwt` instance's algorithm list.

rsa-pkcs1.comment: `RSAAlgorithm(256|384|512)`, all three enabled in the default `jwt` instance.

rsa-pss.comment: `RSAPSSAlgorithm(256|384|512)`, all three enabled in the default `jwt` instance.

ecdsa.comment: `ECAlgorithm` instances for P-256/P-384/P-521 plus ES256K on secp256k1 (RFC 8812). `prepare_key` checks that the imported key's curve matches the algorithm's curve, so a secp256k1 key cannot be used for ES256.

eddsa.comment: Registered under the single RFC 8037 `EdDSA` identifier (not curve-specific alg names). The underlying OKPKey maps Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448; signing accepts whatever Ed curve the key carries.

jwe-key-management.comment: JWE_ALG_ALGORITHMS also contains ECDH-ES+A192KW, which has no tag in this comparison. The three PBES2 variants are present in the file only as commented-out entries, so password-based key wrapping is NOT available. RSA1_5 is registered but flagged `deprecated`, so it is refused unless the caller passes an explicit algorithm list. Draft algorithms (ECDH-1PU, C20P/XC20P) exist under `authlib/jose/drafts/` but `register_jwe_draft` is never called from `authlib/jose/__init__.py`, so they are unavailable without manual registration.

jwe-content-encryption.comment: The six RFC 7518 content-encryption algorithms. C20P/XC20P are implemented in `authlib/jose/drafts/` but are not registered by the package's default wiring (and XC20P additionally needs pycryptodome).

deprecated-algorithms-available.comment: `NoneAlgorithm` (name "none") and the RSA1_5 key-wrap algorithm are both in the registry with `deprecated = True`; in 1.7.2 `_prepare_algorithm_key` raises UnsupportedAlgorithmError for deprecated algorithms when no algorithm allow-list was given, so reaching them requires an explicit opt-in such as `JsonWebSignature(algorithms=['none'])`. No RSA modulus-size check exists anywhere in the JWS path, so sub-2048-bit RSA keys are accepted.

algorithm-extensibility.comment: `JsonWebSignature.register_algorithm()` / `JsonWebEncryption.register_algorithm()` are public classmethods that accept any JWSAlgorithm/JWEAlgorithm subclass; the built-in algorithm sets are themselves registered through this API. It is also an escape hatch: a custom algorithm registered without `deprecated = True` bypasses the deprecation guard.

rejects-alg-none.comment: In 1.7.2 the module-level `jwt` object pins 14 algorithms (HS/RS/ES/ES256K/PS/EdDSA) with `none` absent, and `_prepare_algorithm_key` rejects any algorithm marked `deprecated` when the caller passed no allow-list — `none` is only reachable via an explicit `algorithms=['none']`. This is a regression-repaired state: CVE-2026-28802 (GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg, published 2026-03-04) reported that a token with `alg: none` and an empty signature passed verification in 1.6.5/1.6.6 (regression introduced in 1.6.0), fixed in 1.6.7.

algorithm-pinning.comment: `from authlib.jose import jwt` gives a JsonWebToken pre-configured with a curated 14-algorithm list (no `none`), and the `alg` is then read from the token header and checked against that list. Callers can narrow it with `JsonWebToken(['RS256'])`, which the docs recommend; the docs also explicitly warn against enabling HS and RS/ES/PS families simultaneously because of the CVE-2016-10555 confusion class.

algorithm-confusion-resistance.comment: Keys are typed classes (OctKey/RSAKey/ECKey/OKPKey) and `OctKey.import_key` refuses raw data starting with any of POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS (`-----BEGIN `, `---- BEGIN `, `ssh-rsa `, `ssh-dss `, `ssh-ed25519 `, `ecdsa-sha2-`), which blocks the textbook RS256→HS256 attack of replaying a PEM public key as an HMAC secret; a JWK dict likewise fails OctKey's required-field check. Rated 3 rather than 4/5 because the default `jwt` instance mixes symmetric and asymmetric families, the guard is a byte-prefix heuristic (raw DER key material would slip past), and Authlib's own docs tell users to supply a key-loader callable instead of relying on the library.

unverified-decode-separated.comment: There is no unverified-decode API at all: `JsonWebToken.decode()` always runs signature verification (or JWE decryption) and raises BadSignatureError on mismatch — there is no `verify=False` flag and no `decode_unverified` helper. Reading claims without verification requires manual base64url parsing by the caller, so the unsafe path is strictly longer than the safe one.

default-claim-validation.comment: `jwt.decode()` verifies the signature and returns a JWTClaims dict without checking a single claim; the documented flow requires a separate explicit `claims.validate()` call. When invoked, `validate()` checks iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat and jti — but only for claims present in the payload or marked `essential` in claims_options. Tagged `none` because the attribute records what happens with no extra configuration, and forgetting `validate()` silently accepts expired tokens.

audience-issuer-required.comment: Neither `decode()` nor `validate()` takes a required audience/issuer parameter. Expected values must be supplied through `claims_options`, e.g. {"iss": {"essential": True, "values": [...]}}; with no options the aud/iss checks are skipped entirely.

clock-skew-configurable.comment: `JWTClaims.validate(now=None, leeway=0)`; leeway is applied to exp, nbf and iat. Default is 0 seconds, and `now` defaults to `int(time.time())`.

constant-time-comparison.comment: `HMACAlgorithm.verify` compares with `hmac.compare_digest(sig, v_sig)` from the CPython stdlib. Asymmetric verification is delegated to pyca/cryptography.

minimum-key-size-enforced.comment: Neither requirement of RFC 7518 §3.2/§3.3 is enforced: RSAAlgorithm never inspects the modulus size, and OctKey accepts a secret of any length (its `generate_key` defaults to 256 bits, but imported secrets are unchecked). The only structural check is the ECDSA curve/algorithm match.

crit-header-handling.comment: `_validate_crit_headers` requires `crit` to be a list of strings, raises InvalidCritHeaderParameterNameError for any entry not in REGISTERED_HEADER_PARAMETER_NAMES (extendable by the caller's `private_headers`, which is the caller-declares-understood escape hatch), and requires each named parameter to be present in the header; `_reject_unprotected_crit` rejects `crit` in the unprotected header per RFC 7515 §4.1.11. This behaviour is the fix for CVE-2025-59420 (GHSA-9ggr-2464-2j32, 2025-09-22), where unknown critical headers were silently accepted.

nested-depth-limits.comment: 1.7.2 caps deserialized input with `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 256000` before parsing (added for CVE-2025-61920, oversized JOSE segments, affected ≤1.6.3) and bounds `zip=DEF` inflation (CVE-2025-62706, decompression bomb, affected 1.6.4, fixed 1.6.5). PBES2 is not implemented at all, so there is no `p2c` iteration cap to assess. Nested JWT is not processed recursively, so there is no recursion depth to bound.

cve-history.comment: Dense recent JOSE advisory history, all patched in current 1.7.2 (checked 2026-07-30): CVE-2026-27962 / GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 (Critical, 2026-03-15) — `deserialize_compact` fell back to the attacker-supplied `jwk` header when the key resolver returned None, ≤1.6.8, fixed 1.6.9; CVE-2026-28802 / GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (High, 2026-03-04) — `alg: none` with an empty signature verified, 1.6.5–1.6.6, fixed 1.6.7; CVE-2026-28490 / GHSA-7432-952r-cw78 (High, 2026-03-15) — JWE RSA1_5 Bleichenbacher padding oracle via distinguishable exceptions; CVE-2025-61920 / GHSA-pq5p-34cr-23v9 (High, 2025-10-10) — DoS via oversized JOSE segments, ≤1.6.3; CVE-2025-62706 / GHSA-g7f3-828f-7h7m (Moderate, 2025-10-10) — unbounded DEFLATE for `zip=DEF`, 1.6.4; CVE-2025-59420 / GHSA-9ggr-2464-2j32 (2025-09-22) — unknown `crit` headers accepted. Further 2026 advisories (GHSA-m344-f55w-2m6j fail-open OIDC hash binding, open redirects, CSRF) affect Authlib's OAuth/OIDC layers rather than `authlib.jose` itself.

security-policy.comment: Published policy asking reporters not to open public issues, with private disclosure to me@lepture.com or via Tidelift coordination. The "supported versions" table is stale (lists 1.1.x / 0.15.x), but GitHub private vulnerability reporting is clearly in use given the repository-published advisories.

independent-security-review.comment: No published third-party audit found for Authlib or its JOSE module; the recent advisories originate from individual researchers rather than a formal audit engagement.

jws.comment: `JsonWebSignature.serialize_compact` / `deserialize_compact` plus the JSON serializations; both signing and verification.

jwe.comment: Full RFC 7516 encrypt/decrypt via `JsonWebEncryption`, including `zip=DEF`; `jwt.encode` routes to JWE when the header carries `enc`, and `jwt.decode` handles the 5-segment compact form.

jwk-parsing.comment: `JsonWebKey.import_key` / `import_key_set` build OctKey, RSAKey, ECKey and OKPKey from JWK dicts, with required-field checks per key type.

jwks-remote-fetch.comment: The `authlib.jose` module contains no HTTP client — it parses a JWKS you have already fetched (`KeySet` / `import_key_set`). Remote JWKS retrieval lives in Authlib's separate OAuth/OIDC client integrations, not in the JOSE component being compared here.

jwks-caching-rotation.comment: Follows from the absence of remote fetching: no TTL/Cache-Control handling and no refetch-on-unknown-kid anywhere in `authlib.jose`. Key rotation is entirely the caller's responsibility.

kid-selection.comment: `create_load_key` resolves the verification key from a KeySet (or a JWKS dict) using the token header's `kid`; `find_encode_key` does the same when signing, picking a random key when no kid is given. Note CVE-2026-27962: before 1.6.9 a key-loader callable returning None caused a fallback to the token's embedded `jwk` header.

jwk-thumbprint.comment: `Key.thumbprint()` implements RFC 7638 (required members plus kty, lexicographically ordered, SHA-256, base64url). RFC 9278 thumbprint URIs are not implemented.

nested-jwt.comment: `decode()` dispatches on the dot count (2 = JWS, 4 = JWE) and returns the claims of that single layer; it does not inspect `cty: JWT` or recursively decode a signed token nested inside a JWE. Signed-then-encrypted tokens require two manual calls.

json-serialization.comment: JsonWebSignature implements compact plus the general JSON serialization (list of headers producing a `signatures` array, i.e. multiple signatures) and the flattened single-signature form.

detached-payload.comment: `deserialize_compact` requires three non-empty segments and offers no API for supplying an external payload; no RFC 7515 Appendix F support was found in the JWS implementation.

unencoded-payload.comment: No RFC 7797 module exists under `authlib/jose/` (only rfc7515–7519, rfc8037 and drafts), and `b64` is not among REGISTERED_HEADER_PARAMETER_NAMES; the payload is always base64url-decoded.

key-generation.comment: `generate_key` classmethods on each key type: OctKey (bit size, via `secrets.token_bytes`), OKPKey (crv, default Ed25519), and equivalently RSAKey/ECKey, exposed through `JsonWebKey`.

x509-header-support.comment: `x5u`, `x5c`, `x5t` and `x5t#S256` appear in REGISTERED_HEADER_PARAMETER_NAMES, so they are permitted in a header and round-tripped, but nothing in `authlib.jose` parses a certificate chain, derives a key from `x5c`, checks a thumbprint or dereferences `x5u`. Tagged "none" because acceptance without processing is not support.

key-input-formats.comment: `AsymmetricKey.import_key` accepts key objects, JWK dicts and PEM/DER/OpenSSH-encoded bytes (delegating to pyca/cryptography's loaders, which transparently handle PKCS#1, PKCS#8 and SPKI structures — not separately tagged since Authlib performs no format-specific handling itself); `as_pem`/`as_der` export. OctKey takes raw bytes but refuses anything that looks like a PEM or SSH key. JWKS via `import_key_set`/KeySet. No PKCS#12 or keystore support.

external-signer-support.comment: No signer abstraction: every algorithm's `sign(msg, key)` expects local key material via `prepare_key`. A KMS/HSM signer could be bolted on by subclassing JWSAlgorithm and calling `register_algorithm`, but nothing first-party exists and no such integration is documented.

framework-integrations.comment: Authlib the distribution ships first-party Flask, Django and Starlette/FastAPI integrations (plus requests/httpx clients), but they are OAuth/OIDC client and provider adapters — `authlib.jose` itself has no framework binding, and since 1.7 those integrations consume joserfc rather than `authlib.jose`.

async-api.comment: All JOSE entry points (`jwt.encode`/`decode`, JWS/JWE serialize/deserialize, key import) are plain synchronous functions; there are no coroutines in the module.

typed-claims.comment: JWTClaims is a dict subclass — custom claims are dynamic keys with no static typing. A runtime `claims_options` mapping ({"essential": ..., "values": ..., "value": ..., "validate": ...}) and a pluggable `claims_cls` give some schema-like validation, but only for claims the caller enumerates.

crypto-backend.comment: The sole crypto dependency is pyca/cryptography, whose wheels statically link OpenSSL; HMAC uses CPython's stdlib `hmac`/`hashlib`. XC20P (draft, unregistered) would additionally need pycryptodome.

pure-language-implementation.comment: `requires_dist` is cryptography and joserfc; pyca/cryptography ships a compiled Rust/OpenSSL extension, so the default configuration is not pure Python.

runs-in-browser-wasm.comment: Not determinable from primary sources: Authlib's own code is pure Python, so browser/WASM viability rests entirely on whether pyca/cryptography is available in the target (e.g. a Pyodide build). Neither Authlib's docs nor its packaging metadata make any statement about WASM targets.

edge-runtime-compatible.comment: Not applicable — Authlib is a CPython server-side library (requires_python >=3.10) and the Cloudflare Workers / Vercel Edge / Deno Deploy question is meaningless for this ecosystem, per the comparison's assessment guideline.

fips-capable-backend.comment: Indeterminate: Authlib makes no FIPS statement and offers no backend switch. In practice it inherits whatever pyca/cryptography links against — the published wheels bundle a non-validated statically-linked OpenSSL, while a source build against a system OpenSSL FIPS provider is a deployment-level choice outside Authlib's control. Not verified against a pyca/cryptography FIPS statement, so recorded as unknown rather than false.

dependency-count.comment: `requires_dist` for Authlib 1.7.2: `cryptography` and `joserfc>=1.6.0` (checked 2026-07-30). Only `cryptography` is used by the `authlib.jose` module itself; joserfc is pulled in for the non-deprecated code paths.

package-size.comment: Size of the published wheel authlib-1.7.2-py2.py3-none-any.whl (sdist is 166,874 bytes). This covers the whole Authlib distribution — OAuth 1/2, OIDC and framework integrations — not just the JOSE module.

github-stars.comment: Snapshot of authlib/authlib on 2026-07-30. Counts the whole Authlib project, not the JOSE module specifically.

downloads.comment: PyPI downloads in the last 30 days for the Authlib distribution (checked 2026-07-30; last week 35,609,978). Attributable to the whole package — Authlib is a common transitive dependency — so this overstates JOSE-module usage. Compare only within the Python ecosystem.

last-release.comment: Authlib 1.7.2, 2026-05-06 (1.7.1 on 2026-05-04, 1.7.0 on 2026-04-18). Repository pushed_at 2026-07-30, so development continues after the release.

maintenance-status.comment: Both tags apply and the combination is the point: the Authlib package is actively developed (commits on 2026-07-30, three releases in April–May 2026, advisories patched quickly), but the `authlib.jose` module itself is deprecated — importing it emits "authlib.jose module is deprecated, please use joserfc instead." and the docs state "Changed in version 1.7: ... It will be removed in Authlib 1.8." New code should use joserfc, by the same author.

bus-factor.comment: Last 50 commits (checked 2026-07-30) are spread across azmeuk (~10), lepture (~7), liudonggalaxy (~5), levinKaus (~4) and others, with the rest merge commits. Historically a solo project by lepture; azmeuk is now the most active committer.

maturity.comment: 1.0+ with a stable API, nine years of history and very broad production deployment, and there is a real security process. Not rated `mature` because of the 2025–2026 run of serious JOSE advisories — notably the `alg: none` verification regression introduced in 1.6.0 (CVE-2026-28802) — and because the module is now slated for removal in 1.8.

rfc-conformance-testing.comment: tests/jose contains test_jws, test_jwe, test_jwk, test_jwt, test_rfc8037, test_chacha20 and test_ecdh_1pu. Spot-checking test_jws.py and test_rfc8037.py found only project-local fixtures ("hello"/"secret" payloads, local PEM key files) — no RFC 7515 Appendix A payloads, no RFC 7520 cookbook vectors and no Wycheproof integration. Round-trip and interop-with-self testing rather than spec-vector conformance.

documentation-quality.comment: Dedicated guide pages for JWS, JWE, JWK and JWT with runnable examples plus an API reference, and an explicit security note about not mixing HS with RS/ES/PS (CVE-2016-10555). Short of 5: no JWKS/key-rotation workflow, no consolidated security-considerations chapter, and the fact that `claims.validate()` must be called separately is easy to miss. Every page now opens with a deprecation banner pointing at joserfc.
